paras: The threatened lynching of McBride took place at Waterloo, Monroe County, Illinois, in late January 1882, when a crowd gathered near the jail holding a young pupil accused of stabbing his schoolteacher to death. The crowd threatened to lynch him but made no attempt to do so, and no one was harmed. The killing of the teacher was carried widely as a crime item, while the threat at the jail appeared in a single regional paper, and no report gives the race of anyone involved.

Robert Bailey taught at a school near Red Bud, a station on the Cairo & St. Louis narrow-gauge railroad in Monroe County. According to a wire report printed on January 23, he was stabbed to death on Saturday by James E. McBride, a 17-year-old pupil he was attempting to chastise "for breach of discipline." A weekly digest instead dated the stabbing to the 20th and named the pupil Emmet McBride, saying he "stabbed him to the heart."

The Cairo Bulletin, which named neither party, said the pupil was 18, resisted bodily punishment, and in the struggle stabbed the teacher with "a sharply pointed lead pencil." In its account the teacher bled to death within a few minutes.

McBride was arrested and taken to Waterloo on Sunday, January 22. There he waived examination and was committed to jail to await the March term of the circuit court, though the earliest wire report had him held in $5,000 bail for the grand jury. On the following Monday, by the Cairo Bulletin's account, "a large and excited crowd assembled near the jail and threatened lynching, but they did not attempt to carry out their threats." The paper did not say whether that Monday was January 23 or January 30, how many people gathered, or whether officers dispersed them.
No report of a trial at the March term, or of any outcome in the case, appears in the coverage.

Every report found came from the white press, and none mentioned race. The stabbing travelled as a short wire paragraph, appearing in a Delaware daily on January 23 and in weekly crime digests in Minnesota and Wisconsin on January 25. A filler version that called both teacher and pupil "of excellent character" ran in the Newberry Herald in South Carolina in February and was still being reprinted in Seattle in May.

Only the Cairo Bulletin, reporting from southern Illinois, followed McBride to the Waterloo jail, and it gave the threatened lynching a single sentence in a column of local items. That sentence neither condemned nor endorsed the crowd and stressed only that it did not act.

The reports differ on the pupil's first name (James E. or Emmet), his age (17 or 18), and the day of the stabbing (Saturday the 21st or the 20th). No local Monroe County paper was found to settle these points.

framing.detail: The Cairo Bulletin noted the threat in one flat sentence, adding only that the crowd 'did not attempt to carry out their threats'.
